titleStmt.title: Simulation-based Schedulability Tests for Multiprocessor Real-time Systems

analytic.title: Simulation-based Schedulability Tests for Multiprocessor Real-time Systems

div.p: The assimilation of multiprocessor programming into the real-time application's domain is limited because there are not enough theoretical and pragmatic tools for proving the feasibility of such systems. Theoretical results are few and tend to be too complex for a practical implementation. In this paper, we combine theoretical analysis results with simulation to obtain a tool, which can assess the multiprocessor real-time schedulability of periodic task sets. We performed simulations on different scenarios in order to determine the features that influence schedulability of a multiprocessor real-time system.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: For many decades, the exponential increase in computing performance (see Moore's law) was mainly achieved through higher integration ratio and increased clock frequency on single CPU systems. However, in the last years as the clock frequency reached a saturation level, developers are looking for different parallel solutions in order to preserve the constant increase in computer performance. Real-time system designers must cope with this new challenge of using parallel and distributed computer architectures as support of new applications. Different from general-purpose applications, in the real-time domain parallelization brings more issues than solutions [1]. In uniprocessor systems, the real-time feasibility problem was well studied and there are important theoretical results that offer the designer the analytical support needed for a reliable design [2]. For instance, there are optimal scheduling solutions for static and dynamic priority-based, periodic and sporadic task systems. A designer can evaluate the feasibility of a given task set on a platform using analytical equations and schedulability tests.

Multiprocessor scheduling, on the other hand, still raises open research problems. Most research efforts were, at first, directed towards adapting the most successful uniprocessor scheduling techniques to multiprocessors. The same wellestablished workload models such as the periodic and sporadic (sequential) task models were chosen for analysis. As multiprocessor platforms introduces new variables, many uniprocessor research results proved inapplicable to multiprocessors. For instance, the multiprocessor variants of RM and EDF algorithms are proved to be not optimal.

For this reason, the goal of our research is double: to develop some methods and tools in order to evaluate the feasibility of real-time systems on multiprocessor platforms and to analyze the factors that influence the efficiency of parallel architectures in case of real-time applications. As a corollary of these efforts, we are looking for new scheduling strategies on multiprocessor systems that can increase the chance of finding a feasible schedule.

In this paper, we try to demonstrate that simulation is a possible way of demonstrating the feasibility of a task set on a parallel architecture and a useful tool for statistical evaluation of parallel real-time systems in different load scenarios.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II presents related work. The system model, the terminology and the notation used is introduced in section III. Further on, in section IV, we present the theoretical results used as a basis for the conducted research. Section V introduces our simulation tool and simulation methodology. In section VI we describe the conducted experiments and we analyze the simulation results of multiprocessor global EDF algorithm in different scenarios. Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In the last years, important research efforts were made in the direction of finding feasible scheduling strategies for parallel architectures, but the results are far from being final or stable. One conclusion of these efforts is that the simple extension of uniprocessor theory and experience to parallel systems is not a successful approach. There are many examples when researchers based their demonstration on uniprocessor system results and proved to be wrong on parallel systems. For instance it was proved that in case of a parallel architecture the critical time interval is not the period that follows after all the tasks are released at the same time, as in the case of a single CPU. In addition, the optimality of Rate Monotonic (RM) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithms on parallel systems is not true, at least in some cases.

New optimal multiprocessor scheduling algorithms such as the Proportionate Fair algorithm [3] and its variants [4,5] are almost impossible to be implemented in practice due to very large overheads introduced by their very frequent scheduling decisions and task preemptions.

In the direction of feasibility analysis most of the results concentrate on finding necessary or sufficient conditions for feasibility. Nevertheless, these conditions are in most cases too complex [6] and hard to implement in practice or the gap between the necessary and sufficient condition leave too many cases undecided. The existing sufficient schedulability tests introduce very strong constraints, which excessively limit the utilization factor of many systems. Through simulation, we will show that these feasibility limits are too high and we can find schedulable tasks sets that are not verifying the sufficient conditions.

Another research direction is based on the computation of demand and supply functions for multiprocessor real-time systems. In [7] and [8] the authors derive sufficient conditions for the feasibility of task systems using these functions. The complexity of the obtained relations, as well as the pessimistic results limit the use of this method.

Recent research on priority-based multiprocessor scheduling showed that fixed priority algorithms (including RM and EDF) generate periodic schedules in the case of feasible periodic task systems [9,10]. This result will be used later in section V in order to demonstrate the feasibility of a task set using the simulation approach.

Following these results, we focused our research on combining simulation with theoretical analysis results to assess the schedulability of synchronous periodic task systems. The main objectives of our research are to:
• Develop a methodology for assessing the multiprocessor schedulability of periodic task systems through simulation.
• Experiment the behavior of multiprocessor systems with global EDF using randomly generated periodic task sets, in order to determine the features that influence the shedulability.

The outcome of our work will help real-time system designers to choose a practical strategy that does not involve complex mathematical analysis and which is well suited to the characteristics of their application.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this section, we provide the description of the system model and the definitions of the terms we are using.

In this paper we focus on applications which can be modeled as periodic tasks with no restrictions other than realtime ones. A task set (τ) comprises n tasks and each task (τ i ) is described by its execution time (C i ), repetition period (T i ), and relative deadline (D i ). The relative deadline of a task can be implicit, when it is equal to the repetition period, constrained, when it is less than or equal with repetition period, or arbitrary, when it can have any value.
The hyper-period of a task set is equal to the least common multiple (LCM) of the tasks' repetition periods. This period is important for schedulability evaluation.

At the end of a task's repetition period, a new instance of the task, a job, is released for execution. The release time of the first job generated by a task is called phase. If the phase is equal for all tasks, the task set is called synchronous. If the phases are different, the task set is asynchronous. We consider that all jobs are sequential, meaning that a job has no multiple threads and it can be executed on at most one processor at the same time.

The utilization factor (u i ) of a periodic task is the fraction of processor time spent in the execution of that task [2] (u i =C i /T i ). The total utilization (U) of a task set is the sum of all task utilizations (U=∑u i ).

The platform is modeled as a homogeneous multiprocessor P={P 1 , P 2 , … , P m } composed of m processors with identical characteristics. On a homogeneous multiprocessor the execution rate of all tasks is the same on each individual processor.

The scheduling model describes how the applications use the available resources for execution. In multiprocessor systems, the scheduling problem is double. The scheduler has to establish the execution order of jobs and to assign a given job to a processor.

From the allocation point of view, there are three main approaches for multiprocessor scheduling: global, partitioned and clustered. In the global approach, jobs can be allocated to any available processor and can migrate to other processors during execution, with no restrictions. In partitioned scheduling, each task is assigned to a single processor, and migration to other processors is not allowed. Finally, in the clustered approach, the processors are grouped into clusters, and tasks are assigned to clusters. Migration is allowed only inside a cluster.

In our previous work [12] we made a statistical comparison between the three approaches, using simulation. We also proposed a hybrid scheduling approach, which improved the performance of partitioned and clustered approaches.

For the research presented in this paper we use the global scheduling model which assumes the existence of a unique global scheduler and a global job queue. At each time instant, the global scheduler chooses from the job queue, m a jobs with the highest priority, where m a is the number of available processors. The chosen jobs will be executed on the processors. The priority of each task is computed by using a specific algorithm.
The system scheduler uses a scheduling algorithm to establish the order in which jobs are executed on the platform. A priority-based scheduling algorithm establishes a priority for each job.

Fixed Task Priority (FTP) algorithms assign a priority for each task; the priority is inherited by its jobs. This priority does not change during execution (example: RM). Fixed Job Priority (FJP) algorithms assign a priority for each job. This priority does not change during execution (example: EDF). Dynamic Priority algorithms assign priorities for each job, which are recomputed at each time t during execution.
A task set is considered feasible if there is a schedule so that all tasks are executed without missing any of their deadlines.

A task is A-schedulable according to algorithm A if its worst-case response time obtained with this algorithm is less or equal to its deadline. A task set is A-schedulable if all its tasks are A-schedulable.

A schedulability test assesses the schedulability of a task set according to a given algorithm. The schedulability test is sufficient if all task sets that satisfy the condition are schedulable. The schedulability test is necessary if all task sets that do not satisfy the condition are not schedulable. A schedulability test is exact if it is at the same time necessary and sufficient.
To guarantee the correctness of a real-time system, one has to prove through schedulability analysis that each job will finish its execution before its deadline.

div.head: IV. THEORETICAL RESULTS ON GLOBAL EDF SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: The purpose of this section is to present the theoretical background of our schedulability test methodology and also to have a comparison reference for the experimental results. In this paper, we analyzed the case of synchronous task sets executed on a homogenous multiprocessor system and scheduled with global EDF algorithm.

Most of the theoretical results on global EDF algorithms establish necessary or sufficient conditions for feasibility. In [6] the authors surveyed the most important seven sufficient schedulability tests with different computational complexity levels. One sufficient feasibility test [8], given below, states that a task set is schedulable with global EDF if:

This rather simple condition takes into account only the number of processors m and the usability factor u max of the most demanding task from the set (the task with the maximum utilization factor). It can be seen that if u max is close to 1 the usability of m processors is reduced to the usability of a system with a single processor. We used equation (1) as a reference for the simulation results. A more powerful global EDF schedulability test (in terms of the detected number of schedulable task sets) [6] is based on an iterative method and has a pseudo-polynomial computational complexity. This test computes the minimum slack S k (distance between the deadline and the completion time of a job) for each task. If the slack is negative for a task, the task set fails the schedulability test. The equation is:

According to the latest studies there is a large region between the sufficient and necessary conditişons, where task sets' schedulability is undecided (see Fig. 1). The region increases with the number of processors. For instance, in the 8 processor scenario, this interval starts at a total utilization of approximately 4.5 (about 56% of the maximum utilization). This means that all evaluated schedulability tests introduce strong constraints on the task sets they assess, leaving outside their limits a large number of task sets which may be schedulable.
In our research, through simulation, we want to show that a large number of task sets from the undecided region are in fact schedulable.

Our method is based on the results in [9] and [10], where the authors show that deterministic fixed priority algorithms generate periodic schedules in the case of feasible periodic task systems. In [9] the authors prove that a feasible schedule obtained using deterministic global EDF of a synchronous constrained deadline system on m identical processors is periodic with a period P that begins at instant 0. The schedule repetition period P is equal to the hyper-period. The authors extend their results in [10], where they give an exact schedulability test for global EDF on multiprocessors. To decide if a task set is schedulable, the authors suggest to build a schedule and check if the periodic part of the schedule is reached or not. The periodic part is reached when the execution states at the two ends of the interval coincide (this is true because it is assumed that the algorithm is deterministic). If there are no missed deadlines in the first period, then the task set is schedulable. In the case of asynchronous task systems, the periodic part of a feasible schedule may begin after more than one hyper-period.
In order to test the feasibility of task sets, we implemented a multiprocessor real-time simulator which can assess the schedulability during the task set's hyper-period.

div.head: A. The Simulation Tool
div.p: To support our research on real-time multiprocessor scheduling models and algorithms, we developed RTMultiSim, The simulator implements mainly the system model presented in section III. The workload can be described as a set of periodic sequential or parallel tasks. The multiprocessor is modeled as a sum of identical processing units (CPUs). Delays caused by cache memory transfers are not considered. Job context switch time and job migrations can be taken into consideration if the user chooses to. Usually, it is considered that context switches and migrations add a constant value to the overall execution time.

The simulation time is modeled as a global clock. All CPUs are synchronized to this clock. The global clock advances with one simulation time unit (STU). At each clock tick (transition), the state of the system is recomputed. There can be new job releases and, depending on the scheduling strategy, there can be schedule updates that generate preemptions.

The job execution time is equal to an integer number of STUs. Each CPU executes exactly one STU from the total execution time of a job, and then the schedule is updated. After that, the current executing job can be preempted or it can continue its execution. The simulator's scheduler implements the clustered approach. In this approach, the tasks are allocated to clusters (groups) of processors and then, tasks are globally scheduled on each cluster. Global and partitioned approaches are particular cases of clustered scheduling. When the cluster is extended to all processors we have global scheduling, and when the cluster contains only one processor we have partitioned scheduling.

Our scheduler contains a global temporary job queue and a list of scheduling groups (SGs), one SG for each cluster. At the start of the simulation, a partitioning algorithm is applied to assign all tasks to a particular SG.

A scheduling group contains the assigned task set, the cluster (group of CPUs), a global job queue and a scheduler that globally schedules the jobs on the CPUs in the cluster. It is important to notice that we implemented a hierarchy of schedulers. The schedulers at the bottom of this hierarchy can use different scheduling strategies.

Each newly released job is added to the clustered scheduler's temporary queue. The clustered scheduler forwards the job to one SG according to task partitioning. Then, the job waits to be scheduled on the SG's cluster.

The simulation results are periodically written in a database, which records each simulation separately, with its executed jobs. Jobs may have one or multiple threads. For each thread, release, start and completion time are recorded. The sequence of visited CPUs is also recorded for each thread.

div.head: B. Task Set Generation
div.p: Task sets used for empirical evaluations are generated automatically in the majority of cases. The method used to generate tasks is essential, as some task set characteristics like the task set cardinality, the distribution of task periods or the distribution of individual task utilizations may influence the evaluation, which produces misleading results. To give an example on how task parameters may influence evaluation results, we generate task sets with 10 tasks and a total utilization of 4.8. We simulate their execution on a multiprocessor composed of 6 identical processors with global EDF. In the first case we use a random distribution of task utilizations. In the second case, we limit the values of task utilizations in the interval [0.38, 0.58], very close to the mean value (0.48). While about 60% of the task sets generated in the first case will register deadline misses, all task sets generated in the second case will not register any deadline misses.

Our objective is to obtain task sets which will not influence the outcome of our simulations. To generate a task set with n periodic tasks with implicit deadlines and utilization U, we developed the following methodology:
1. Randomly choose n task periods (T i ) uniformly distributed in the interval [T min , T max ], having the LCM less than a given LCM max .

2. Generate n random utilization values (u i ) for which the sum is equal to a given U. Each u i has to be equal or greater than 1/T i (because the computed execution time C i has to be greater than 0) and less than 1.
3. For each pair (T i , u i ), compute the execution time C i =u i *T i of task i.
4. Verify if the task set satisfies the requested parameters.
If not, the task set is discarded.

The algorithm in Fig. 2 generates n utilization values with the sum equal to U. It starts with assigning each u i the mean value (U/n). To obtain a random distribution of the utilization values inside the task set and keep the total utilization equal to U, at each step we randomly choose two u i values which will be modified by adding and subtracting a random value from the interval [0,U/n]. After a large number of iterations, we obtain task utilization values, which are well spread in the interval [1/P i , 1].

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: During the experiments, we want to evaluate the dependencies between the schedulability of a task set and the following factors: number of processors, number of tasks in a set and total utilization.

div.head: A. Simulation Scenarios
div.p: We conducted experiments with global EDF algorithm for different systems and determined through simulation which of the generated tasks sets are schedulable. We made simulations in 4 cases, with 2, 4, 6 and 8 processors. For each case we generated synchronous periodic implicit deadline task sets with increasing cardinalities between m+2 and m*10, and increasing total utilizations between 0.6*m and 0.99*m, where m is the number of processors. We created 30 task sets for each individual scenario. For each task set we selected task periods from the interval [10,250], having the LCM less than 100,000. The total number of task sets generated and simulated was approximately 10,000.

We use synchronous periodic tasks with implicit deadlines, so the schedule period will start at time 0 and will be equal to the task set's hyper-period. To decide if a task set is schedulable in a specific scenario, the system is simulated in the task set hyper-period. If there aren't any deadline misses, then, according to the results presented in section IV, the system is schedulable.
On each of the generated task sets we also applied the global EDF schedulability test described by equation (1), in order to compare the results with those obtained with the simulation-based method.

div.head: B. Results Analysis
div.p: Evaluating the results, we made the following observations:

1. As expected, the schedulability of a task set decreases with the increase of its total utilization. This can be seen in Fig. 3a and Fig. 4a, where for 2 and 8 processors the number of not schedulable task sets is represented related with the total utilization factor.

2. For a given total utilization, the most critical scenarios are when the number of tasks in a set is slightly higher than the number of processors; as the number of tasks increases the number of not schedulable tasks decreases, becoming equal to 0 when the number of tasks is more than 10 times the number of processors.

3. For the same number of processors and total utilization, the schedulability depends on the distribution of individual task utilization. Fig. 5a shows 3 distribution cases: two approximately uniform distributions (case 1 and case 2) and an exponential distribution (case 3). The results in Fig. 5b show that a uniform distribution is better, causing a smaller number of failing task sets. The results are the best when the individual task utilization values are in a smaller interval (case 1).

4. The results obtained through simulation are more optimistic than those obtained for the same scenarios using the analytical sufficient schedulability conditions. Fig. 3 and 4 compare the two situations; in Fig. 3a and 4a are results obtained through simulation and in Fig. 3b and 4b are results obtained with equation ( 1). This observation motivates the use of our simulation-based methodology.

5. The schedulability of a task set is more critical when there are a few tasks with utilization close to 1. From Fig. 5 case 3 we observe that if we have task utilizations in the interval close to 1 the schedulability deacreases. This is somehow in accordance with equation (1).

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we analyzed the schedulability of task sets on multiprocessors, scheduled with global EDF. The proposed methodology is based on simulation. We showed that there is an important gap between theoretically determined necessary and sufficient schedulability conditions, which can be overcome through simulation. Experimental measurements made on different kind of task set distributions revealed the dependency between schedulability, utilization factors and number of tasks. The conclusion of these experiments is twofold. For a given total utilization, an increased number of tasks increases the feasibility chance. The presence of tasks with utilization close to 1 reduces the chances for the whole set to be schedulable. The results obtained through simulation proved to be more optimistic than the theoretical ones.
